title: Matsya, the fish in Manu's hands
word: the ten avatars as a series
hookLine: a fingertip fish asks a praying king to keep it safe
carry: the lord can come as the smallest creature
tomorrow: the fish says a flood is coming. what goes in the boat?

cards: What if the Lord of everything came small enough to fit in your hands? Early morning, at the water: a king named Manu is cupping water in his hands to offer it, and there's something in his palms.
A fish, no bigger than a fingertip. It speaks. Please, it says, keep me safe.
In the water, the big fish eat the small ones. That's the whole reason, and it's enough for Manu.

teach.h: A FISH IN A WATER JAR.
teach.b: That's how the Matsya Purana opens the story, and the Bhagavata Purana tells it too, where the king is called Satyavrata.
Manu was in the middle of a prayer, offering water, the way many Hindus still pour water as an offering each morning. He doesn't toss the fish back. He takes it home and puts it in a water jar.
By the next day it has outgrown the jar. He moves it to a pool, and it fills that.
A lake, then a river, and each time the fish grows to fill the space it's given.

teach.h: THE ONE WHO FILLS EVERYTHING, MADE SMALL.
teach.b: At last he brings it to the ocean, and it fills even that. Only then does Manu ask who it is. It is Vishnu, the first descent in the row.

Here's the teaching inside it. This is what Hindus mean by an avatar: God coming down into a shape we can meet. Vishnu's name is often explained as the one who pervades everything; no jar can hold him.
Yet he comes first as the smallest thing there is, asking for help.

teach.h: THE LORD LIVES IN EVERY BEING.
teach.b: In the Gita, Krishna says, in paraphrase, that the Lord lives in the heart of every being. So a creature in your hands is never just a creature.

It's one reason many Hindu families set out food for birds or cows before they eat. And notice: Manu cared for the fish before he knew who it was. Then, in the ocean, the fish tells him why it came: a flood is on its way.

how: Matsya's story is retold from the Matsya and Bhagavata Puranas in homes and temple talks, and he is pictured as the first of Vishnu's descents, often as a fish below and Vishnu above. Many Hindus offer water each morning, and many families set out food for birds or animals before a meal.

games.q: what does “the ten avatars as a series” mean?
o: Vishnu's descents in a row, with the fish first
a set of ten temples along a sacred river
ten stories of kings rescued from a flood

games.q: the little fish — tap the pairs.
p: cups water and finds a tiny fish
a flood is on its way

s: Matsya appears as a giant fish from the very first moment
he begins no bigger than a fingertip, in Manu's cupped hands.
the fish asks for protection because big fish eat small ones
that's the whole reason it gives, and Manu takes it in.
Manu knew the fish was Vishnu from the start
he cared for it first, while he was praying; he asks who it is only after it fills the sea.

games.q: an ant is crossing the kitchen counter. your little cousin goes to squash it, and Nani scoops it onto a leaf and carries it outside. 'why??' by Matsya's story?
o: the Lord lives in every being; a tiny fish turned out to be Vishnu.
ants are bad luck if you kill them indoors.
Nani just doesn't like a mess on the counter.
games.why: Manu kept a fingertip fish safe before he knew it was Vishnu. Hindu teaching says the Lord lives in the heart of every being, so even an ant is worth carrying outside.

practice: If you have a cup of water, hold it in both hands, the way Manu held the river water, and pour a little, slowly, onto a plant or the ground outside, as many Hindus pour water as a morning offering.
While it pours, bring to mind one small creature or person in your care. If you don't pray, simply water the plant and notice who depends on you.

wordCard.voice: The ten avatars as a series: Vishnu's descents in a row, and Matsya, the fish, comes first.

orig.note: Sanskrit matsya: fish. The name of Vishnu's first descent, and of the Purana that tells it.

carryVoice: Something to keep: the Lord can come as the smallest creature, asking to be kept safe. Day done.

sources.ref: Matsya Purana 1–2 (Manu finds the fish; it outgrows each vessel; the warning of the flood)
Shatapatha Brahmana 1.8.1 (the older telling of Manu and the fish)
Bhagavad Gita 18.61 (the Lord dwells in the heart of all beings)
